newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Kalimantan riot not an issue in Indonesia campaign.
newsitem.headline: Kalimantan riot not an issue in Indonesia campaign.

text.p: The three political parties contesting Indonesia's general elections said on Tuesday that the bloody ethnic riots in West Kalimantan province earlier this year were not an issue in the campaign.

At least 300 people are believed to have died in fighting in the province between Borneo's ethnic Dayaks and migrants from Madura Island, off eastern Java. The clashes started in late December and continued into February.
"They (the riots) are not a issue in the election," said Sutarmidji, one of the leaders in Pontianak of the minority United Development Party (PPP).

Leaders of the PPP and the other two parties legally entitled to contest the May 29 polls -- the ruling Golkar and the Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI) -- said the campaign, now in its third week, had been peaceful in the sprawling, heavily forested province at the western end of Borneo island.
The PPP campaigned through Kalimantan on Tuesday as part of the agreement by the three parties not to campaign in the same area on the same day.
Golkar will campaign in Kalimantan on Wednesday, including a rally at Sanggau in the heart of the riot-hit area, about 300 km (200 miles) east of the provincial capital Pontianak.

Golkar's secretary-general in the province, Petrus Djuman, told Reuters the Dayaks and the Madurans had reached a peace agreement to end the riots. But Djuman, a Dayak, conceded that 5,000-6,000 Maduran refugees were still in the Pontianak area, afraid to return to their homes in the countryside.

He said the death toll from the fighting was estimated at 300. The military has said only 12 people were confirmed killed. An Indonesian youth forum that sent a team to the remote area in February said some 1,200 people were missing after the violence.
The PPP held a series of small rallies, each of 100 or so supporters, on Tuesday thoughout Pontianak, a bustling port of about 450,000 people on the Kapuas river.
The PPP's Sutarmidji said the party hoped to add two seats to the five it won at the last elections in 1992. At that time, Golkar won 23 seats and the PDI eight.
Nationwide, 425 seats in the 500-member parliament are at stake. The other 75 seats are filled by the military, which does not vote.

Sutarmidji said he expected the party to pick up votes from former supporters of PDI, which split last year after Megawati Sukarnoputri, the daughter of late founding president Sukarno, was ousted as party chief by a government-backed faction.
On the main island of Java, Megawati's supporters have begun attending PPP rallies in large numbers and analysts say they are likely to vote for the Moslem-based party.
But the PDI in West Kalimantan appears not to have been affected by the split, although its leaders appeared cited a lack of funds as an election problem.
The headquarters of the three parties dramatically illustrated the differences in funding.
Golkar's headquarters is in a large and ornate building opposite the provincial parliament and has computers, photocopiers and fax machines.
The headquarters of the other two parties are shabby storefront offices in the commercial area, equipped with a few old typewriters and little else other than enthusiasm.
"We don't have much money," Edy Suryanto, a PDI vice-president in Pontianak, told Reuters. "If we had more money, it would not be so difficult to campaign."
